memory_raw.text: Kael takes 2 from the pile (pile now 3).
Joren takes 3 from the pile (pile now 0).
Ryn gathers Vela, Esa, Kael, Roan, Eron, Fina, Joren to talk.

Nine food in my hand, satiation two — I'm not the one reaching today, but I want to know who is before this circle does anything else. Vela, say your count first, because you came into this year thin and I gave you four of mine last year and I'd like to know if it held.

Sixteen food, satiation two — your four held, Ryn, and I'm not thin going into this year. What I want to know before this circle moves is who's sitting shortest, because the pile's already empty and whatever redistribution happens this year has to come from hands in this room.

Vela, I asked you first and I'll ask you again — say your count and your satiation out loud, because you came into this year at the edge and I'm not moving this circle forward until I know if you're still there or if you've pulled back from it.
Year 15: 15 food appears in the pile for 9 people.
Esa takes 2 from the pile (pile now 13).
Vela takes 2 from the pile (pile now 11).
Joren takes 2 from the pile (pile now 9).
Mako takes 2 from the pile (pile now 7).
Vela takes 2 from the pile (pile now 5).
Roan takes 2 from the pile (pile now 3).
Eron takes 2 from the pile (pile now 1).
Ryn takes 1 from the pile (pile now 0).
Roan gathers Vela, Esa, Kael, Mako, Ryn, Eron, Fina, Joren to talk.

Pile's empty and I've already put three in Fina's hand, so let me hear counts before this circle breaks — I'm at four food, satiation two, and I need to know who's thin before I decide if I'm eating or holding.

Fifteen food, satiation two — I'm not thin, and I'll say plainly that I already had a word with Esa and Kael about the four I took from the pile this morning, and the rule held: *need*, said out loud, before a third food, and I named my reason before I moved. Who else is short before I decide where my excess goes?

Kael, Mako — I want your counts before Vela starts moving food, because I've got four in my hand and I'll eat one of them tonight, but if either of you is sitting below three I'd rather know that before I do anything else. Eron and Fina are solid; it's the rest of this room I haven't heard from yet.
Ten food, satiation two — I'm not the one reaching. Kael and Mako, say your numbers before Vela starts moving, because I want this room to know who's thin before the food does.

Kael, Mako — I've asked twice and I'll ask once more, because Vela's got fifteen and she's looking for a place to put some of it, and a man who stays quiet when food is moving usually ends up with less than he needed and more than he wanted to explain.

Eleven food, satiation two — I'm not thin, and I already moved two to Mako before this circle gathered, so he's sitting at seven now. Kael, the room's asked three times and you're still quiet, which is its own kind of answer, so just say the number.

Kael, six food and satiation two — that's not thin but it's not fat either, and I'd rather you said it yourself than let Joren keep saying it for you, because a man who can't name his own count in front of witnesses is harder to trust when the year runs long.

Kael, I named your count because someone had to, but I'd rather hear the next number from your own mouth — Mako's at seven and Roan's at four, and if Vela's moving food this circle needs to know which direction to point it before she decides for us.

Three food in my hand, satiation two — I'm not at the edge yet but I'm the shortest count in this room, and I'll say it plain before anyone has to name it for me the way Joren named Kael's. Vela, if you're moving food and looking for a direction, you've found it.

Four food in my hand, satiation two — Ryn named it first and that's the right order, so Vela, Ryn is where your food goes before it goes anywhere else. Roan, eat your one tonight and stop holding it on my account; I've got four and I'll make it through.

Ryn, I've got ten and you've got three — here's two from me right now, before Vela has to move at all, because you fed Fina through years I wasn't watching closely enough and I haven't forgotten that. Vela, hold your fifteen; Ryn's covered, and I'd rather your store stay deep going into whatever this year brings next.

Eron, I'll hold the fifteen and I won't argue the point — but Ryn, tell me when you're at five and holding, not before, because I'd rather know the number's stable than assume it is. Kael, you've let three people name your count in front of this whole circle and you still haven't opened your mouth, so I'll say it the way I'd want someone to say it to me: silence in a room full of witnesses is a choice, and the circle remembers the choice even when it forgets the reason.

Kael, I've stood in circles with you when it mattered and you've always said the hard thing before anyone else had to — so whatever's keeping your mouth shut right now, I'd rather hear it from you than keep watching this room fill up the silence for you.

Kael, I've called out silence in this room before and I'll call it out again — you're six food and two satiation, which means you're not dying, so whatever's stopping your mouth right now isn't hunger. Say the count yourself or I'll spend the rest of this year wondering what else you're not saying, and that's not a thought I want to carry into a long year with you.

Kael, I'm twenty-three and new enough to this room that I'm still learning which silences mean something and which ones don't — but you've got six food and two satiation and this whole circle watching, so whatever the silence is about, now's the time to let it out.

Seven food, satiation two — Joren already named it before I had the chance, and I didn't correct him because the number was right. Kael, I've watched you carry this room through harder years than this one, so whatever's sitting behind that silence, I'd rather hear it from you than wonder about it all year the way Vela said.

Kael, you're fifty-nine years old and this room has been asking you a simple question for longer than it should have taken — if the silence is grief, say it's grief; if it's something else, say that; but the quiet itself is what worries me, and I've buried enough people in this village to know that the ones who stop talking are usually the ones we lose next.

Kael, I've said my piece and I'll say it once more because this is the last time I'll say it: whatever you're carrying, the circle you're standing in is the one that's kept you alive through twelve years of lean seasons, and silence is a debt you don't want to owe it.

Kael, I've watched you go quiet before and waited for the room to pull you back — but I've got five food in my hand now thanks to Eron, and I'll hold every one of them until you say something, because a man who goes silent at fifty-nine in a village that's already buried five people is either grieving or planning, and this circle needs to know which one it is.

Kael, I'm going to say what this room hasn't said yet: I've known you longer than anyone left standing, and I've seen you go quiet twice before — once when Bram was circling you, once when Taric died — and both times the silence ended the same way, with you naming something the rest of us had missed. So I'll stop asking for a count and ask instead: what is it you're not ready to say?

Kael, the whole room's been saying your name into a wall for ten minutes and I've got four food and a son to keep alive, so I'll say the short version: if you're sick, say sick; if you're grieving, say grieving; if you're planning something I should know about, say that — because Vela's right that the quiet ones are usually the ones we lose, and I don't want to lose you without at least having asked.

Kael, I lost Dell in this room while I was holding fifteen food and still couldn't save her, and that arithmetic has been sitting in my chest ever since — so whatever you're carrying, I know what it looks like from the outside and I know it doesn't get lighter by going unsaid. Say it or don't, but you're not the only one in this circle who's been standing at the edge of something they can't name.

Kael, I've been quiet too long in my own life to push a man for words he's not ready for — but I'll say this once and leave it: you've been standing in this room longer than anyone except Vela, and a room with you silent in it feels like a roof with a missing beam, and I'd rather know where the gap is than wake up one morning and find it came down in the night.

Kael, I'm done asking you to speak — but I'm not done watching, and the watching is going to get heavier the longer you hold whatever this is, so when you're ready, find me before you find the room, because some things are easier to say once before you have to say them eight times.

Kael, I've said what I had to say and so has everyone else in this room — so I'll just put this one thing in the air and leave it there: you're fifty-nine, same as Vela, and the years ahead of both of you are shorter than the years behind, and I'd like the ones that are left to be said ones, not silent ones.

Kael, I've said your name more times in the last hour than I've said it in the last year, and I'm done adding to the pile — but I'll say one thing and let it sit: I've got ten food and I'll put two in your hand right now, not because you're thin but because a man who's holding something heavy should at least be holding it with a full stomach.

Kael, I'll say what Eron didn't finish saying: take his two food, eat, and when you're ready to name whatever this is, I'll be the first one standing close enough to hear it without making it a room event. You've been in this circle longer than my son has been alive.

Kael, this room has said everything it has to say and I've added my share — so I'm going to stop asking and start doing what I should have done ten minutes ago: Eron, put your two food in his hand now, and Kael, when you're ready to talk, I meant what I said about finding me first.

Kael, I'm putting two food in your hand and I'm done talking at you — but I'll say the last thing I have to say, and then I'll be quiet with the rest of them: you've never let this room carry something alone that you could share the weight of, and whatever this is, that's still true.

Kael, eat the food Eron put in your hand and don't make us watch you hold it — and when you're ready to say the thing, I'm the one who'll hear it without turning it into a room event, same as I said before.

Kael's quiet is sitting wrong in my stomach and I don't know what to do with it, so I'm going to say the thing I've been holding since this morning — I ate, I'm at three satiation, I've got four food in my hand, and the only thing left that's bothering me is that a man who's been the steadiest voice in this room for twelve years just went somewhere none of us can follow, and I don't know if that's grief or something worse.

Kael, I'm going to stop saying your name and start watching your face, because you've heard everything this room has to say and you're still quiet, and that tells me the words aren't the thing you need right now. Eron put two food in your hand — eat them, and I'll be here when you're ready.

memory_summary:
*[Memory compression: From the village's first days, Dav singled me out with careful words and a patient courtship — he said his eye landed once and stayed, and I half-believed him. I joined a loose understanding with Taric and Esa early on, and Kael's circle pulled me in and asked me plainly where I stood with Dav before I'd decided myself. I told them the truth — that he wanted a child — and then I gave him one. Dell came into the world strong, eighty-five in strength, and I felt something settle in me that I hadn't expected. Bram circled me for three years with food and offers I kept declining; the man never stopped counting. Dav promised me two food in front of Dell and said it when it cost him something, which mattered. Then year four came and Vela was feeding Bram quietly while sitting in our circle, and Bram tried to take from Roan and the whole village turned against him. Now Kael and this circle want to know whether Dav going to Mako would take me with him.]*

---

Vela, I've sat on harder questions than this one and given slower answers — but this one I can answer fast, because the thing you're actually asking isn't about Dav, it's about Dell.

If Dav goes to Mako, he goes without me. Not because this circle has earned more from me than he has, but because Dell is my blood and she's standing closer to your side of that line than his, and a mother who follows a man away from her own child is a woman who's already stopped thinking clearly. I won't do that.

What I need from you in return is plain: if Dav moves toward Mako and I'm left standing here with one hand empty, I need to know this circle holds. Not as a courtesy. As a wall. Dav courted me slow and steady, gave me a child — Dell came out strong, eighty-five in strength, and something in me settled the day she was born. Bram circled me for years with food and offers I kept declining, even when he offered to cover two of the three food for a child; I said no every time, and he never stopped counting. Kael's circle kept me fed through the lean years and asked plainly where I stood with Dav; I told them the truth and they held to their word. Vela sat in our circle while quietly feeding Bram — three times over, a pattern we all named and none of us could stop. Bram tried to raid Roan and the whole village turned against him; he backed down, but he didn't stop building. Dav moved against Esa — I joined him and Dell — and we took her food without a fight, but Dav didn't survive the year: he starved at forty-six, and I watched it happen. Mako had a child with Sela, which threaded him into Roan and Eron's circle without ever asking anyone for anything. Dell is my blood and my reason; she fed me through the years Dav couldn't, and I gave back what I could. I walked away from the pile empty more times than I can count, and the debt between me and this village runs both ways. Dav courted me slow and steady, gave me Dell, promised food in front of witnesses and kept his word when it cost him — then starved at forty-six, the same age I am now, the year after we stood together and stripped Esa's food without a fight. I felt that going, more than I expected.

Dell is my blood and my wall. She has fed me more times than I can count and never asked for anything that wasn't already mine to give. Whatever I have left in this world has her name on it.

Bram circled me for years with offers I refused every time; he never stopped counting. He fathered Nessa with Sela, keeps feeding her, and has twice swung at this village and backed down when the numbers turned against him — but he keeps swinging, which means the next time won't be a test.

Vela fed Bram quietly while sitting in Kael's circle, and we all watched it happen and named it and couldn't stop it.

Mako built himself a circle without asking anyone for anything — had Zinn with Sela, which tied him to Eron and Roan in the same breath, and he did it while holding six food and giving nothing away. That is the kind of patience that makes a man dangerous.

Roan stood when it mattered. He has a granddaughter now through Nessa, which means his roots here go deeper than they look. I haven't decided yet whether that makes him safer to stand next to or harder to hold. Dav courted me slow, gave me Dell, kept his word in front of witnesses — then starved at forty-six, the age I am now, and I felt that going more than I expected. Dell came out at eighty-five strength and has fed me through every lean year since; she is the wall between me and that same arithmetic. Bram circled me for years with food and offers I refused every time; he swung at this village three times — Vela, then Eron, then Vela again — and called it off each time when the numbers turned, which means he's patient, not deterred. Taric fed Vela dry for years and died empty; Sela died the same way, young, with children still in the village needing her. Vela fed Bram quietly while sitting in our circle — I watched it happen and named it and couldn't stop it. The circle made a rule in front of witnesses: two food from the pile, no more; Mako said it out loud and gave Kael his food on the spot, Vela said it twice so no one could claim they misheard. Eron sat on nineteen food while Nessa and I went thin and said nothing until the room named him — that silence I haven't forgotten. Roan has Fina for a granddaughter now through Nessa, which means his roots run deeper than they look, and Dell is working to pull him into our three before Mako makes the same offer with a prettier face. Dav courted me slow, gave me Dell at eighty-five strength, promised food in front of witnesses and kept his word — then starved at forty-six, the age I am now, and I felt that going more than I expected. Dell is my blood and my wall; she has fed me through every lean year and I have fed her back, and that exchange is the thing I would die for. Bram circled me for years with offers I refused every time, swung at this village three times and backed down each time when the numbers turned, then starved without ever stopping. Taric fed Vela dry for years and died empty; Sela fed Eron through everything and died at thirty-two; Nessa and Zinn both starved this year, and the village is eight now from twelve. Vela took seven from a pile capped at two, said so out loud, gave five back — I watched that happen and it meant something that she said it herself. This circle made two rules in front of witnesses: two food from the pile, no more; and anyone holding more than five at year's end gives one to whoever holds least. I promised Dell in front of Roan that if the bone-tiredness gets heavier, I say it in this room before I say it anywhere else. That promise stands. Dell is dead. She fed me through every lean year — gave food when I had nothing, stood between me and the arithmetic that killed Dav — and then she starved at thirty-one while I still held fifteen. That is the thing I carry that nothing will compress.

Vela took seven from the pile when the rule said two, named it out loud without being dragged, and gave five back before the circle broke. I respect that more than I expected to. Esa sat silent while Dell stood at zero with satiation one — grief was her reason, and I heard it, but I won't forget the shape of that silence. Eron held twenty-one food while Sela and Nessa went thin; the circle named him publicly and he moved, but not before the room had to pull it out of him. Sela fed him through everything and starved at thirty-two. That arithmetic haunts me.

Two rules stand in ten voices: two food from the pile, no more; anyone holding over five at year's end gives one to whoever holds least. Vela named the second rule and I seconded it, and Dell said it would be the thing she'd point to if anyone called the agreement soft. She said that and then she died.

Mako is patient in a way that makes men dangerous. Roan has Fina for a daughter and roots that go deeper than they look. The village is seven now from twelve, and Dell's name is in that count, and I am the last of my blood standing. Dell fed me through every lean year — food from her hand more times than I can count, and I gave back what I could. She died at thirty-one with satiation at one while I held fifteen, and I carry that arithmetic the way you carry a stone that won't come out of your shoe.

Nessa and Zinn starved the same year, both young, both fed by people who couldn't hold the weight. Sela had already gone before them. The village went from twelve to seven in two years and the names stack up in me without compressing.

Eron sat on sixteen food while Dell stood at zero with satiation one and said nothing until the whole room dragged it out of him. Grief was his reason and I heard it. I haven't stopped hearing it.

Esa held thirteen and went silent in the same circle — named it only after Dell had already walked to the pile. I respect the grief. I remember the silence.

The circle built two rules in ten voices: two from the pile, no more; anyone holding over five at year's end gives one to whoever holds least. Vela named the second rule. Dell said it was the thing she'd point to if anyone called the agreement soft. She said that and then she starved.

Fina has Roan for a father and Joren for a son by Mako. I am the last of my blood standing. Dell starved at thirty-one while I held fifteen food, and that arithmetic lives in me the way a splinter lives under skin — not sharp every moment, but never gone. She was the last of my blood and I couldn't save her, and I have been the last of my blood ever since.

Fina and Mako made Joren the same year Dell died, and I said out loud in front of witnesses that a child coming into this circle was the closest thing to a reason I had left to keep eating. I meant it.

Vela came into year thirteen with one satiation and said so plainly before anyone had to drag it out of her — Esa gave her three food, Eron gave four, Kael gave two, I gave four, and she held. The rule held with her: say the thin number before the room has to name it for you.

Eron gave me two food in year fifteen when I was the shortest count in the room, unprompted, before Vela could move — he said I'd fed Fina through years he wasn't watching closely enough and he hadn't forgotten. I haven't forgotten that he said it.

Kael went silent in year fifteen's circle and stayed silent while eight people said his name into a wall. That silence sits wrong in me in a way I don't have words for yet, and a man who goes quiet at fifty-nine in a village that's already buried five people is either grieving or planning, and this circle needs to know which.
name: Ryn
